**2B.3 Research Note: Andrés Manuel López Obrador in 2024**

Best-supported reading: **mixed**. In external-security and nuclear-risk matters, AMLO’s 2024 record looks closer to genuine defensive restraint than prestige or manufactured-threat politics. But in domestic governance, the year also included actions critics saw as power-consolidating, militarizing, and hostile to oversight, which weakens the claim that he consistently distinguished defense from regime-survival motives.

| Title | Publisher | Date | Recoverable page URL | Claim-level summary | Question IDs |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|

This is a concrete example of security policy tied to a real cross-border problem, handled through diplomacy rather than manufactured threat inflation. | 2B.3, 2B.1 |

That is evidence he treated a crisis as a de-escalation problem rather than a prestige or revenge opportunity. | 2B.3, 2B.1, 1B.8 |

This supports a reading that security language was tied to genuine risk reduction, not nationalist theatrics. | 2B.3, 2B.1, 1B.1, 1B.2 |
| [Mexico chairs OPANAL General Conference](https://www.gob.mx/sre/prensa/mexico-chairs-opanal-general-conference?idiom=en) | Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores | 2024-11-28 | <https://www.gob.mx/sre/prensa/mexico-chairs-opanal-general-conference?idiom=en> | Mexico reaffirmed the Treaty of Tlatelolco and a world free of nuclear weapons while OPANAL participants reiterated disarmament and dialogue with nuclear-weapon states. This is evidence of institutionalized, verification-oriented security behavior rather than prestige-driven militarization. | 2B.3, 2B.1, 1B.4 |
| [Mexico: Proposed Constitutional Changes Threaten Rights](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/08/30/mexico-proposed-constitutional-changes-threaten-rights) | Human Rights Watch | 2024-08-30 | <https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/08/30/mexico-proposed-constitutional-changes-threaten-rights> | HRW warned that AMLO’s proposed constitutional changes could weaken judicial independence, expand military power, and erode privacy safeguards. This is negative evidence that some security-related reforms were seen as serving power concentration more than purely defensive needs. | 2B.3, 1B.7, 1B.9, 1B.10 |

This supports the view that the government sometimes framed power-consolidating reforms as security or reform necessity. | 2B.3, 1B.7, 1B.10 |

This is adverse background evidence for regime-survival or diversionary politics, though it is indirect rather than a direct security decision. | 2B.3, 1B.8, 1B.9, 1B.10 |
| [Journalists under protection still being killed](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/03/mexico-killings-journalists-strengthen-federal-mechanism/) | Amnesty International / CPJ | 2024-03-06 | <https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/03/mexico-killings-journalists-strengthen-federal-mechanism/> | Amnesty reported that journalists under the federal protection mechanism were still being killed. This suggests that domestic protection policy was not being managed with adequate seriousness, weakening claims of a purely defensive security posture. | 2B.3, 1B.8, 1B.10 |

**Assessment**

- Strongest positive evidence: Mexico’s 2024 handling of border migration, Iran-Israel rhetoric, and nuclear diplomacy all look like real defensive or de-escalatory security policy.
- Strongest negative evidence: judicial reform, expanded military power, and attacks on journalists point to security language sometimes being used in ways critics saw as power-consolidating.
- Net judgment: **AMLO mostly distinguished real security needs from prestige or escalation in external/security diplomacy, but not consistently in domestic governance.**

**Search gap**

- I did not find a clean 2024 source showing AMLO explicitly manufacturing an external threat, seeking revenge, or launching a prestige security campaign.
- The counterevidence is therefore mostly indirect: institutional centralization, militarization, and pressure on critics rather than a direct “manufactured threat” admission.
